cards.front: Define the minor $M_{ij}$ of an element $a_{ij}$ in a matrix.
cards.back: The minor $M_{ij}$ of an element $a_{ij}$ is the determinant of the submatrix formed by deleting the $i$-th row and $j$-th column of the original matrix.

cards.front: Define the cofactor $C_{ij}$ of an element $a_{ij}$ in terms of its minor $M_{ij}$.
cards.back: The cofactor $C_{ij}$ of an element $a_{ij}$ is given by the formula $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$. The term $(-1)^{i+j}$ determines the sign of the cofactor.

cards.front: State the general formula for the determinant of a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ using cofactor expansion along the $i$-th row.
cards.back:
For a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$, the determinant can be calculated by cofactor expansion along any row $i$ as: $$\det(A) = \sum_{j=1}^{3} a_{ij}C_{ij} = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + a_{i3}C_{i3}$$
Alternatively, along any column $j$: $$\det(A) = \sum_{i=1}^{3} a_{ij}C_{ij} = a_{1j}C_{1j} + a_{2j}C_{2j} + a_{3j}C_{3j}$$

cards.front: Calculate $\det \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ using cofactor expansion along the first column.
cards.back:
Expanding along the first column:
$\det(A) = 1 \cdot C_{11} + 0 \cdot C_{21} + 5 \cdot C_{31}$
$C_{11} = (-1)^{1+1} \det \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = (1)(1 \cdot 0 - 4 \cdot 6) = -24$
$C_{21} = (-1)^{2+1} \det \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = (-1)(2 \cdot 0 - 3 \cdot 6) = (-1)(-18) = 18$ (but this term is multiplied by $a_{21}=0$, so it's $0 \cdot 18 = 0$)
$C_{31} = (-1)^{3+1} \det \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = (1)(2 \cdot 4 - 3 \cdot 1) = 8 - 3 = 5$
$\det(A) = 1(-24) + 0(18) + 5(5) = -24 + 0 + 25 = 1$.

cards.front: When calculating a $3 \times 3$ determinant using cofactor expansion, what strategy minimizes calculations?
cards.back: To minimize calculations, choose the row or column that contains the most zero entries. This is because any term $a_{ij}C_{ij}$ will be zero if $a_{ij}=0$, effectively reducing the number of $2 \times 2$ determinants you need to compute.

cards.front: Briefly explain why expanding a $3 \times 3$ determinant along any row or column always yields the same result.
cards.back: The determinant of a matrix is a unique scalar value that satisfies certain axiomatic properties (e.g., multilinearity, alternating property, and $\det(I)=1$). The cofactor expansion is a method to compute this unique value. While the expansion can be performed along any row or column, the underlying mathematical properties ensure that all valid expansions will lead to the same, unique determinant value for the given matrix.
